statementMappings.statement: {patientName}, a 57-year-old woman, attends the clinic to review outside records of persistent right-hand symptoms with the founder.
The founder and {patientName} review the next dated outside-clinic record.
Nighttime tingling affects the thumb, index and middle fingers; placing the wrist in flexion reproduces it.
The report lists ulnar motor conduction across the elbow and needle sampling of first dorsal interosseous; these were normal.
Symptoms continue despite a neutral wrist splint; a hand surgeon has requested objective localization before an intervention.
Which study should be obtained to complete {patientName}'s pre-intervention hand evaluation?
Median conduction across the wrist
The symptom map suggests a wrist-level median process, but the outside study evaluated a different nerve and segment. A targeted median study addresses that gap.
If the prior report already contained an adequate concordant median assessment, repeating it merely because the ulnar study was normal would add little.
Ulnar conduction across the elbow
This repeats the documented normal territory rather than assessing the symptomatic wrist-level median segment.
Little/ring-finger symptoms reproducible at the elbow would make this segment relevant.
Median conduction across the forearm
A forearm-segment assessment does not directly test the suspected wrist-level conduction abnormality.
A proximal median-territory motor deficit would justify an assessment directed beyond the wrist segment.

A normal result applies to the nerve and segment actually examined. The symptom map and the prior study scope together justify median testing at the wrist; a positive history is not itself an order to operate.
{patientName}, a 57-year-old woman, attends the clinic to review outside records of persistent right-hand symptoms with the founder.
The founder and {patientName} review the next dated outside-clinic record.
The interpreting physician documents focal median conduction slowing at the wrist with reduced thenar motor response; sampled proximal muscles are preserved.
The thumb cannot lift away from the palm against resistance, and the thenar contour has become visibly flatter.
The wrist splint and a prior carpal-tunnel corticosteroid injection gave only temporary relief; numbness and hand clumsiness are worsening.
Which treatment plan should be recommended for {patientName}'s worsening hand deficit?
Hand-surgical assessment for carpal tunnel release
Concordant focal testing, progressive motor loss and failed nonsurgical care support surgical assessment rather than another symptom-only trial.
Intermittent sensory symptoms improving with splinting and preserved motor function would favor continued nonsurgical care.
Another carpal-tunnel corticosteroid injection
A prior temporary sensory response does not address the new progressive motor deficit.
A patient with a stable sensory-predominant presentation could reasonably consider an injection after discussing its temporary effect.
Another trial of neutral wrist splinting
The current motor and functional deterioration outweighs the rationale for extending the same unsuccessful initial measure.
A new mild presentation without motor loss that responds to splinting would support this plan.

Worsening motor function changes the decision after localization. Surgical assessment is appropriate; this item does not choose an operative technique, predict complete recovery or impose a fixed symptom duration.
{patientName}, a 48-year-old man, attends the clinic to review outside records of right elbow and hand symptoms with the founder.
The founder and {patientName} review the next dated outside-clinic record.
Little/ring-finger tingling accompanies prolonged elbow flexion; finger spreading has become weaker.
An averaged ulnar motor velocity across a long elbow segment was reported normal. Needle examination found abnormalities in ulnar intrinsic muscles but not in sampled non-ulnar muscles.
Pressure behind the medial epicondyle reproduces the familiar tingling; neck movement does not change it.
Which electrodiagnostic assessment best resolves the remaining localization question for {patientName}?
Short-segment ulnar studies at the elbow
A short focal abnormal segment can be diluted by a longer normal segment. More local sampling addresses the discordance.
If the symptomatic and abnormal territory were confined to the wrist, elbow segment testing would no longer be the main target.
Repeat averaged ulnar studies over the same span
The same averaging can miss the same short focal segment. The symptom/examination data warrant a more localizing approach.
A documented technical artifact in the first acquisition could justify repeating that same acquisition after correction.
Median studies across the wrist segment
The clinical and needle findings center on an ulnar process, not a median wrist process.
Thumb/index/middle symptoms and a concordant median-pattern motor examination would make this target appropriate.

Interpret a normal averaged result in the context of the actual acquisition. Short-segment ulnar assessment can reveal a focal elbow lesion. No conduction cutoff or numerical sensitivity claim is required.
{patientName}, a 48-year-old man, attends the clinic to review outside records of right elbow and hand symptoms with the founder.
The founder and {patientName} review the next dated outside-clinic record.
Short-segment studies now localize focal dysfunction at the elbow.
Tingling and a palpable snap occur as the elbow moves from extension into flexion; neither occurs with the arm held still.
A stored resting ultrasound shows no mass; it contains no flexion/extension acquisition.
Which imaging study best addresses {patientName}'s remaining elbow symptoms?
Dynamic elbow ultrasound during flexion and extension
The unresolved issue is movement of the nerve or adjacent structures. A resting image does not test the symptomatic maneuver.
A persistent deep fixed mass would instead require imaging directed at defining that lesion.
Repeat resting elbow ultrasound in extension
Another static acquisition repeats the condition in which the event does not occur.
A newly palpable resting mass could justify targeted static reassessment.
Static elbow MRI with the arm extended
A static MRI may define masses but does not best reproduce the observed motion-dependent nerve event.
A suspected structural mass or deeper lesion unresolved by ultrasound could make MRI appropriate.
The prior scan answers a resting structural question. Symptoms linked to elbow motion require dynamic assessment; finding nerve movement does not by itself select a specific operation.
{patientName}, a 52-year-old woman, attends the clinic to review outside records of postoperative right-shoulder dysfunction with the founder.
The founder and {patientName} review the next dated outside-clinic record.
An outside posterior-triangle cervical lymph-node excision preceded a new lower resting shoulder and reduced overhead reach.
Resisted shoulder shrug is weak. The medial scapular border does not lift during forward pushing; active glenohumeral abduction is stronger when the scapula is manually supported.
Needle testing of deltoid and biceps was normal.
Which additional electrodiagnostic target is most useful for {patientName}'s current shoulder deficit?
Needle examination of trapezius
The neck operation and weak shrug implicate trapezius function. Normal deltoid and biceps do not directly assess that motor territory.
Dominant medial-border winging on forward pushing with preserved shrug would instead prioritize serratus sampling.
Needle examination of serratus anterior
The dominant deficit is weak shrug and shoulder droop, rather than the forward-push pattern of serratus weakness.
Medial winging accentuated by forward pushing with preserved shrug would support this target.
Repeat needle examination of deltoid
The prior normal sample did not evaluate the muscle implicated by weak shrug and scapular support response.
A new glenohumeral abduction deficit with an axillary-territory examination could justify deltoid assessment.
The negative test is specific to the sampled muscles. A trapezius-directed evaluation addresses this postoperative motor pattern; the findings do not establish transection or prescribe repair.
{patientName}, a 46-year-old man, attends the clinic to review outside records of postoperative right-shoulder dysfunction with the founder.
The founder and {patientName} review the next dated outside-clinic record.
Shoulder fatigue and loss of forward reach began after an outside axillary node procedure.
The medial border lifts away from the chest on forward pushing. Shrug is strong, and passive shoulder elevation remains full.
The report describes normal trapezius and deltoid needle samples.
Which additional electrodiagnostic target best addresses {patientName}'s current shoulder deficit?
Needle examination of serratus anterior
The examination implicates serratus-supported scapular motion. The normal sampled muscles do not test that territory.
A dominant weak shrug with shoulder droop and preserved pushing would prioritize trapezius assessment.
Repeat needle examination of trapezius
The preserved shrug and already normal trapezius sampling do not address the untested forward-push deficit.
New weak shrug and shoulder droop would redirect assessment to this muscle.
Repeat needle examination of deltoid
The abnormal scapular motion during pushing points away from repeating a glenohumeral muscle sample.
New isolated glenohumeral abduction weakness could justify this target.

The symptomatic motor territory must be examined. The forward-push findings and preserved shrug support serratus-directed testing rather than another already normal sample; no recovery timeline or operative indication follows from this item.
{patientName}, a 64-year-old woman, attends clinic after an outside admission for right-knee symptoms. The founder reviews the dated hospital decisions with the patient.
The founder and {patientName} review the next dated outside-hospital record in clinic.
The right native knee was swollen and warm, with a palpable effusion and marked pain throughout passive motion. Fever and an elevated CRP were recorded.
Blood pressure, mentation and peripheral perfusion remained normal; no organ dysfunction was documented.
Blood cultures had been collected. The medication record showed analgesia but no antimicrobial administration.
Which initial outside-hospital plan best fit {patientName}'s knee presentation at this stage?
Aspirate the knee, then start empiric antibiotics
The joint findings warrant urgent microbiologic sampling. In this stable recorded stage, sampling before antibiotics avoids unnecessary loss of diagnostic yield.
New shock or infection-related organ dysfunction would make antimicrobial treatment urgent rather than waiting for joint sampling.
Start empiric antibiotics, then aspirate the knee
The record supplies a stable opportunity for joint sampling; giving antibiotics first can compromise microbiologic confirmation.
Sepsis or shock would justify urgent antibiotics while sampling is pursued without delaying treatment.
Obtain knee MRI, then aspirate the knee
The clinically evident effusion can be sampled without first resolving a structural MRI question. MRI-first postpones the key microbiologic step.
An anatomically difficult or poorly localized deep-joint problem or suspected adjacent disease could require imaging-directed assessment.

Concerning native-joint findings require synovial microbiology. The stable systemic observations permit joint sampling before empiric antibiotics. The sequence changes when sepsis makes treatment delay unsafe.
{patientName}, a 64-year-old woman, attends clinic after an outside admission for right-knee symptoms. The founder reviews the dated hospital decisions with the patient.
The founder and {patientName} review the next dated outside-hospital record in clinic.
The fluid was cloudy, with numerous neutrophils and monosodium urate crystals. The Gram stain showed no organisms; cultures were still incubating.
The patient remained febrile with severe pain on passive knee motion and persistent effusion after aspiration.
Empiric intravenous antibiotics had been started after sampling.
Which interim treatment plan best fit {patientName}'s knee while cultures were pending?
Continue empiric antimicrobial treatment
Crystals and a negative Gram stain do not exclude infection. The ongoing inflammatory joint/systemic course sustains concern while microbiology is unresolved.
A subsequent adequate negative infection evaluation with a resolving crystal-driven course could support stopping antimicrobials and treating the crystal disease.
Replace antimicrobials with oral colchicine
The crystals explain a competing inflammatory process but do not settle whether infection also exists.
Once infection is adequately excluded and the course fits crystal arthritis, crystal-directed treatment may be appropriate.
Replace antimicrobials with intra-articular steroid
Injecting steroid does not address the unresolved infectious possibility in a persistently febrile painful joint.
A confirmed noninfectious inflammatory joint process after adequate infection evaluation could justify local steroid treatment.

Interpret crystals and Gram stain within the whole record. Neither finding safely closes the infectious branch here; maintain the empiric plan while cultures and urgent orthopedic reassessment continue.
{patientName}, a 59-year-old man, attends clinic after an outside admission for right-knee symptoms. The founder reviews the dated hospital decisions with the patient.
The founder and {patientName} review the next dated outside-hospital record in clinic.
Intravenous antibiotics were administered at the referring hospital before the first knee aspiration.
The first fluid culture remained negative after the laboratory completed routine incubation; repeat fluid was again cloudy and neutrophil-rich.
Pain on passive knee motion, effusion and fever persisted during treatment.
Which additional laboratory test best addresses {patientName}'s unresolved knee findings?
Bacterial PCR on synovial fluid
Antibiotic exposure before sampling can limit culture recovery. Synovial molecular testing addresses persistent microbiologic uncertainty.
Without ongoing infection concern or prior antibiotic exposure, molecular testing would not automatically outrank routine studies.
Repeat Gram stain on stored synovial fluid
Another stain is less useful than adding a molecular method to this already culture-negative antibiotic-exposed workup.
A newly obtained initial fluid sample still needs a Gram stain as part of its standard microbiologic assessment.
Repeat crystal microscopy on synovial fluid
Crystals cannot settle the persistent concern for a bacterial process after antibiotic-exposed negative cultures.
A primary crystal-arthritis question after infection concern has resolved would make microscopy central.
The treatment-before-sampling sequence limits what a negative culture establishes. Synovial PCR can add information in this setting; its result still requires interpretation with the clinical record.
{patientName}, a 59-year-old man, attends clinic after an outside admission for right-knee symptoms. The founder reviews the dated hospital decisions with the patient.
The founder and {patientName} review the next dated outside-hospital record in clinic.
The synovial bacterial PCR detected S. aureus; the original culture had not produced an isolate.
The laboratory received a small amount of newly aspirated fluid and reported that it could not perform every requested test.
Bacterial culture, leukocyte count and crystal examination were all requested.
Which requested analysis should receive priority for {patientName}'s limited repeat knee aspirate?
Bacterial culture of the new aspirate
Bacterial identification remains the priority when volume is limited. A PCR detection has not provided a viable isolate for standard susceptibility testing.
If culture material were already adequately secured and the remaining problem were crystal identification, microscopy could receive the residual sample.
Leukocyte count of the new aspirate
A numerical inflammatory count cannot substitute for bacterial identification in this unresolved culture workup.
After sufficient microbiology sampling, count/differential can add useful inflammatory context.
Crystal microscopy of the new aspirate
Crystals could coexist with infection and should not displace bacterial identification when fluid is scarce.
If microbiologic needs were already met and the residual clinical question were crystal arthritis, this would become relevant.

Use scarce synovial material to preserve bacterial identification first. The positive molecular result does not create a cultured isolate, and an inflammatory count or crystal result cannot replace it.
{patientName}, a 51-year-old woman, attends clinic after an outside admission for right-knee symptoms. The founder reviews the dated hospital decisions with the patient.
The founder and {patientName} review the next dated outside-hospital record in clinic.
The hospital performed an arthroscopic washout of an infected native knee and started antibiotics active against the recovered organism.
Purulent drainage and a reaccumulating effusion continued; passive motion became more painful, and CRP rose on serial measurements.
The susceptibility report and medication record remained concordant, with no missed antimicrobial doses.
Which next treatment step best fit {patientName}'s knee at this recorded reassessment?
Repeat arthroscopic knee debridement
Persistent purulence, deteriorating function and rising inflammatory markers support failed source control despite an active antimicrobial regimen.
A dry improving knee with falling inflammatory markers would favor continuing treatment rather than repeat debridement.
Change to broader intravenous antibiotics
The available susceptibility and administration record do not identify inadequate antimicrobial activity; the local purulent course requires renewed source-control attention.
A new resistant isolate or documented inadequate antimicrobial activity could warrant a regimen change.
Continue the current intravenous antibiotics
Passive continuation overlooks combined evidence of local treatment failure.
Improving pain, a dry wound and decreasing markers would support the existing plan.

An active antibiotic does not establish adequate source control. The combined local deterioration and inflammatory trend support repeat orthopedic debridement assessment, without claiming that any single CRP value mandates surgery.
{patientName}, a 51-year-old woman, attends clinic after an outside admission for right-knee symptoms. The founder reviews the dated hospital decisions with the patient.
A later outside postoperative record is now reviewed with {patientName} in clinic.
After the repeat knee procedure, lateral-leg tingling appeared. The anesthesia record documented return of strength and sensation after the block before this complaint.
Ankle dorsiflexion and eversion were initially present but became progressively weaker on repeated examinations. Distal perfusion remained intact.
Electrodiagnostic testing obtained near symptom onset was reported normal; the motor deterioration continued afterward.
Which evaluation plan best fit {patientName}'s evolving leg deficit at that outside-hospital stage?
Urgent neurology or peripheral-nerve consultation
Progressive objective motor loss requires urgent assessment despite an early normal study. A fixed interval before repeat EDX must not become a reason to defer clinical evaluation.
Mild resolving sensory symptoms without motor loss could support planned review.
Scheduled repeat electrodiagnosis with later clinic review
A later EDX may become useful, but its timing does not resolve the need to assess current progression.
A stable nonprogressive deficit after initial assessment can have a planned testing/review pathway.
Supervised rehabilitation with routine clinic review
Routine recovery management does not address new progressive motor loss after the block resolved.
Improving symptoms and recovering objective strength after adequate assessment would support rehabilitation follow-up.

Current objective progression takes precedence over an early normal test. Seek urgent neurologic/peripheral-nerve assessment; postoperative timing does not establish which operative, anesthetic or compressive mechanism caused the deficit.
{patientName}, a 62-year-old woman, attends clinic to review outside back-pain records with the founder. The questions refer to dated outside assessments.
The founder and {patientName} review the next dated outside-hospital record in clinic.
Focal lumbar pain persisted at rest and repeatedly woke the patient from sleep.
The patient was afebrile, with unchanged leg strength and sensation. CRP remained above the laboratory reference range.
Lumbar radiographs showed osteophytes and disc-space narrowing without an acute fracture; no cross-sectional spine imaging had been performed.
Which next spine study best fit {patientName}'s initial outside evaluation?
Contrast-enhanced lumbar spine MRI
The infection history and inflammatory course remain concerning despite absent fever and degenerative radiographs. MRI evaluates early vertebral/disc and adjacent soft-tissue infection.
A genuine MRI contraindication requires an alternative imaging strategy for the same diagnostic goal.
Noncontrast lumbar spine CT
CT is useful for bony detail but is not the preferred next assessment of this suspected disc/soft-tissue process when MRI is feasible.
Bony destruction or stabilization planning after infection localization can make CT useful.
Technetium lumbar bone scan
A bone scan is not preferred when MRI can assess the vertebral and adjacent soft-tissue process.
A real MRI contraindication can justify a selected alternative imaging strategy.
Afebrile status and degenerative films do not adequately explain persistent focal pain with continuing inflammatory evidence. MRI addresses the vertebral/disc and adjacent soft-tissue question.
{patientName}, a 62-year-old woman, attends clinic to review outside back-pain records with the founder. The questions refer to dated outside assessments.
The founder and {patientName} review the next dated outside-hospital record in clinic.
MRI showed opposing endplate marrow abnormalities, intervening disc enhancement and adjacent paraspinal inflammation; there was no neural compression or drainable epidural collection.
Blood cultures collected before antibiotics remained negative after routine incubation.
The patient remained normotensive, alert and neurologically unchanged; spine specialists planned nonsurgical treatment.
Which diagnostic-treatment sequence best fit {patientName}'s spinal findings at this stage?
Obtain image-guided disc/endplate samples, then select antibiotics
Stable nonsurgical disease without an identified organism permits targeted microbiology/histology before empiric therapy reduces yield.
New sepsis or neurologic compromise requires urgent treatment/surgical assessment without waiting for this elective sequence.
Start empiric antibiotics, then obtain disc/endplate samples
Stable physiology and negative blood cultures leave a pre-treatment tissue-diagnosis opportunity.
Sepsis would prioritize urgent treatment while microbiologic material is obtained as feasible.
Obtain open operative disc/endplate samples, then select antibiotics
No operative indication or failed image-guided sampling makes open sampling the preferred initial route.
A surgical indication or persistently nondiagnostic less-invasive sampling could justify operative acquisition.

Organism evidence and current stability determine the sampling sequence. Stable culture-negative nonsurgical disease supports image-guided sampling before empiric treatment; deterioration changes the priority.
{patientName}, a 55-year-old man, attends clinic to review outside back-pain records with the founder. The questions refer to dated outside assessments.
The founder and {patientName} review the next dated outside-hospital record in clinic.
The outside team treated culture-confirmed vertebral infection with susceptibility-concordant antibiotics.
The patient was afebrile; pain and walking tolerance improved. Leg strength and bladder/bowel function were unchanged. CRP fell toward the reference range.
The report described more prominent endplate/disc abnormalities but no new epidural collection, neural compression or deformity.
Which treatment response plan best fits {patientName}'s current spinal record?
Continue the planned pathogen-directed treatment
Clinical/inflammatory improvement can coexist with evolving bony MRI abnormalities; the scan does not establish failure here.
New fever, worsening pain, rising markers or a neurologic change would prompt renewed failure evaluation.
Replace treatment with broader empiric antibiotics
The scan does not establish resistance or inadequate treatment during documented clinical response.
A resistant isolate or convincing clinical/microbiologic failure could justify a regimen change.
Proceed to operative spinal debridement
No compression, deformity or clinical failure is documented to supply a surgical indication.
Neural compression, instability or refractory infection could support surgical assessment.

The response supports continuing planned treatment. MRI normalization need not coincide with clinical improvement. New neural or mechanical problems would require a different assessment; no treatment-stop rule is asserted.
{patientName}, a 55-year-old man, attends clinic to review outside back-pain records with the founder. The questions refer to dated outside assessments.
The founder and {patientName} review the next dated outside-hospital record in clinic.
Fever remained absent and CRP continued to fall, but severe focal back pain now appeared on standing and settled when recumbent.
Leg strength, sensation and bladder/bowel function remained unchanged.
A supine CT showed further collapse at the previously infected segment; alignment had only been assessed lying down.
Which next imaging acquisition best addresses {patientName}'s new symptom pattern?
Standing spinal radiographs compared with supine imaging
The new loading pain and collapse raise an alignment question that unloaded images may not resolve.
New neurologic deficit or concern for epidural extension would prioritize urgent neural MRI and surgical assessment.
Repeat supine spinal CT with the same positioning
Another unloaded acquisition does not best test whether alignment changes under load.
An unresolved bony anatomy question for operative planning could justify targeted CT.
Contrast spinal MRI with the patient supine
MRI evaluates infection/neural structures; the new uncertainty concerns loading with unchanged neurology and improving inflammation.
New fever, rising markers or neurologic change strengthens an infection/epidural reassessment indication.
Infection response and mechanical competence differ. Loading pain with collapse warrants assessment of alignment under load; no angle, height-loss or operation threshold is invented.
{patientName}, a 67-year-old woman, attends clinic to review outside back-pain records with the founder. Questions refer to dated outside assessments.
The founder and {patientName} review the next dated outside-hospital record in clinic.
Separate blood-culture sets obtained before antibiotics grew methicillin-susceptible S. aureus, with a complete susceptibility report.
MRI showed contiguous disc/endplate inflammatory abnormalities and adjacent soft-tissue inflammation at the site of focal back pain.
The patient was stable without neural compression or a current operative indication.
Which etiologic treatment plan best fit {patientName}'s concordant spinal and blood findings?
Begin S. aureus-directed treatment using the blood isolate
Typical-organism bacteremia and compatible spinal imaging provide a concordant etiologic basis; a separate diagnostic vertebral biopsy is not routinely required in this exact setting.
Negative cultures, a likely contaminant or discordant imaging would restore the need for tissue diagnosis.
